children: The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) named industry giant International Business Machines to advance to the final stage of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative on Thursday.

Quantum computing is often framed as the next technological revolution, ushering in a generation of ultra-powerful machines that can solve problems beyond the reach of classical computers. Quantum applications are being explored in areas including drug discovery, financial modeling, and supply-chain optimization.

The technical leap remains in the development phase for now. The ultimate goal is to build fault-tolerant quantum systems that can detect and correct errors in real time, much like today's computers. Achieving this milestone is no small feat, as quantum hardware is extraordinarily sensitive to environmental noise like vibrations and temperature fluctuations.

Consequently, the commercial landscape for quantum remains in its infancy. Evaluating opportunities in this space is particularly challenging for investors as they wait for the technology to mature and deliver tangible economic value.

That's where DARPA comes in. Launched in 2024, the agency's quantum benchmarking program serves as an independent audit of its participants' progress toward building an industrially useful, error-corrected system by 2033.

As IBM enters Stage C, independent experts from the agency — an arm of the Defense Department — will move beyond reviewing the company's technical plans to directly testing its quantum hardware and supporting technologies.
Reaching Stage C brings IBM into a "rigorous phase of independent evaluation," according to Oliver Dial, IBM fellow and vice president of quantum systems. "IBM is ready for that test," he added.

The evaluation is just as critical for investors. In an industry rife with grand claims and hype, the Quantum Benchmark Initiative offers an objective look at which companies have the best shot at building utility-scale systems.

Stage C participants could receive up to $300 million from the government if their designs perform as promised. Beyond the capital, DARPA's endorsement provides vital credibility, offering a stamp of approval on IBM's plan to release a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The selection builds on recent momentum, including the launch of IBM's most advanced quantum processor to date and a demonstration proving how chips can be linked to increase processing power.
"We welcome DARPA's independent evaluation and the opportunity to demonstrate why IBM is positioned to start delivering scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers this decade," Dial said.

One notable name was missing from the list: Quantinuum, the Honeywell spinout that went public in June. Quantinuum is frequently cited as a technical leader in the field, making its omission all the more surprising.

In a preprint published earlier this week, researchers at Germany's Jülich Supercomputing Centre used a lightweight, low-resource benchmark to evaluate quantum processors during error correction. The study revealed that Quantinuum's Helios processor outperformed IBM chips in certain operations critical to error correction.

To be clear, Quantinuum hasn't been dropped from the program. A spokesperson told Barron's the company is actively discussing a "Stage C scope of work" with DARPA while continuing to work on its Stage B contract, which centers on research and development.

Quantinuum reiterated that it remains on track to deliver useful quantum systems by the start of the next decade. "We look forward to continuing our close collaboration with DARPA to advance our shared vision for utility-scale quantum computing," the spokesperson said.

Although the initiative can help investors find opportunities in the space, the Quantum Benchmarking Initiative isn't structured as a competition. That sets it apart from a $215 million quantum initiative the Energy Department unveiled last month.

Recent executive orders underscore how these efforts align with a broader U.S. strategy to secure domestic supply chains and corner the global quantum technology market. To that end, the federal government has set an ambitious target to deploy a fault-tolerant, "scientifically relevant" quantum system at a national laboratory by 2028.
